title: On the Effect of Anticipation on Reading Times
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether readers’ expectations about upcoming words influence reading times beyond the standard surprisal effect. The authors argue that reading is not only responsive to already observed words, but also anticipatory: readers may allocate processing time based on how uncertain they are about future words. They operationalize anticipation using contextual entropy and related Rényi entropy measures.

The study compares entropy- and surprisal-based predictors on four naturalistic reading datasets: two self-paced reading corpora (Brown and Natural Stories) and two eye-tracking corpora (Provo and Dundee). The analysis uses GPT-2 small to estimate word-level surprisal and entropy, then fits linear regression or logistic regression models to predict reading times and word skipping. The participants are adult readers, including undergraduate readers in Brown and adult native English speakers in the other corpora, all reading naturalistic English texts in lab-style reading tasks.

The main finding is that contextual entropy often predicts current-word reading times above and beyond surprisal, especially in Brown, Natural Stories, and Dundee, with Rényi entropy (alpha = 1/2) sometimes outperforming Shannon entropy. However, entropy effects are generally local and do not reliably predict spillover in the way surprisal does. The paper finds some evidence that word skipping is associated with entropy, but weaker evidence that entropy effects on reading times are driven by budgeting or preemptive processing. Overall, the authors conclude that reading behavior reflects both responsive and anticipatory processing, but that anticipation appears to matter most for current-word processing rather than later spillover.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic language model / chatbot-style generative AI system producing word probabilities used to compute surprisal and entropy over text.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper uses GPT-2 small as a language-model estimator to approximate word surprisal and contextual entropy in naturalistic reading corpora; it does not study an educational AI product or K-12 learning intervention.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a psycholinguistics paper about reading-time prediction, not an educational intervention study. It uses a language model as an analytic estimator, but does not evaluate an AI tool for K-12 learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 literacy or instructional impact is measured. The reported results concern model fit to adult reading-time data, not learner achievement or educational effectiveness.
